history.title: Look at What Things Are Made Of

data.body:
**Due:** (your teacher will tell you)

Clear glass is useful for windows. Wool is useful for sweaters. This week you find out why, and it turns out there is a rule behind it.

1. Read **Why Windows Are Not Wool** with a partner.
2. Learn the words in **Material Words**, then win the **Matching** game and the **Memory** game.
3. Look at the **Pick the Right Stuff** chart.
4. Play **Which Job Is It For?** and sort the cards.
5. Take **Material Check** — say each answer out loud first.
6. Lock it in with **Remember the Rule**.
7. Read **Material Questions Kids Ask**.
8. Finish with **Investigation: The Spill Test** — compare how three samples behave when they meet water.

Your job this week: pick one thing in your home and say why it is made of what it is made of. 🧱

Picture panels: Materials fit a job; Look closely at properties; Make a fair comparison; Materials around us. Use these alongside the activities.

history.title: Why Windows Are Not Wool
history.data:
## Why Windows Are Not Wool

Look through a clear window. Then feel a soft sweater. Why do people choose different **materials** for these jobs?

A material is what something is made of. Wood, glass, metal, and cloth are materials. 

A **property** is something we can observe or test. Is a sample **hard** or **soft**? Is its surface **rough** or **smooth**? Can we see through it?

Clear glass lets us see outside. It resists dents, but it can still break. Smooth does not always mean see-through: a metal spoon can be smooth too.

A knitted sweater bends with your body. Air held among its fibers helps slow heat escaping from you. Some wool feels soft; some feels scratchy.

A **bendy** strip curves without breaking. A stretchy rubber band gets longer when pulled. Bending and stretching are different.

A raincoat made with **waterproof** material helps keep rain out. A towel needs to **absorb** water, which means take it in. The job helps us choose useful properties.

How do we choose? We **test** real samples. Compare equal-size dry pieces with the same water amount, waiting time, and method. Repeat with fresh dry pieces. Describe what you see.

A damp patch shows where water has spread. A bigger patch does not prove that more water was absorbed. If two samples take in all the water you added, this test cannot tell which could hold more.

Untreated paper towel is useful for spills but poor for a rain cover. A coating can change how paper behaves. Name the exact sample instead of assuming every kind is alike.

Pick an object. What is its job? Which properties help it do that job?

data.title: Remember the Rule
data.instructions: Two cards hold the big ideas. Look at the example, make one your own, then say how it helps you.
data.sourceExcerpt: Choose properties that fit a job. Test specific samples fairly, because coatings, shape, and thickness can change how an object behaves.

cards.target: The material was picked to fit the job
essentialFacts: An object may contain more than one material.
Properties help us decide which sample fits a job.
Shape, thickness, and coatings can change behavior.
No single material is best for every job.
cards.aiExample: FIT THE JOB. Point to a clear window: see outside. Point to a sweater: bend with me and help keep me warm.
cards.mapping: Connect each object to a property that helps it do its job.
cards.scaffoldStarter: This is made of ____. The job needs ____.
scaffoldSteps: Choose a safe object to observe.
Describe a property that helps its job.
coachPrompts: What would go wrong if it were made of wool?
cards.studentPrompt: Make your own short phrase for the rule.
cards.reasoningPrompt: How does your phrase help you when you meet a new object?

cards.target: The two opposite jobs water can give a material

history.meta: 3 groups • 9 cards • sort by the main job; objects may have several useful properties

questions.question: Why is clear glass useful for a window?
options: It lets us see outside and resists dents
Glass costs less money than wool does
Wool had not been invented when windows were made
Glass is the only material anyone knows how to shape
questions.correctAnswer: It lets us see outside and resists dents

questions.question: A towel and a raincoat both meet water. What is different?
options: A towel keeps water out; a raincoat soaks it up
A towel soaks water up; a raincoat keeps it out
They both soak up water, just at different speeds
They both keep water out, so either one works
questions.correctAnswer: A towel soaks water up; a raincoat keeps it out

questions.question: What is a property of a material?
options: The place where somebody first found it
The price a shop asks you to pay for it
Something you can notice about it, like hard or soft
The name of the person who made it first
questions.correctAnswer: Something you can notice about it, like hard or soft

questions.question: Is paper a good material or a bad one?
options: Good, because you can draw and write on it
Bad, because it tears and gets wet so easily
Good, because it can be made into almost anything
Neither; it fits some jobs and not others
questions.correctAnswer: Neither; it fits some jobs and not others

questions.question: Which plan makes a water comparison fairer?
options: Give more water to your favorite sample
Use different sizes and compare after different times
Use equal-size dry samples, equal water amounts, and the same waiting time
Use a wet sample for one material and a dry one for another
questions.correctAnswer: Use equal-size dry samples, equal water amounts, and the same waiting time
questions.conceptLabel: a fair test changes one thing

questions.question: Pick something in the room. Say what it is made of and why that material fits its job.
questions.expectedAnswer: Answers vary. A full answer names the object, names the material, and names at least one property that matches what the object has to do, such as a chair being made of hard wood so it holds you up.

questions.question: Your friend wants a rain cover made of untreated paper towels. What would you explain?
questions.expectedAnswer: Paper towels take water in and may soak through or tear. A rain cover needs to keep water from passing through. We should test a suitable coated or waterproof sample for that job.

reflections.text: What is one thing you touched today, and what is it made of?
What material would you like to test, and what job would you test it for?

history.title: Material Questions Kids Ask

data.question: Can something be hard AND bendy? 🤔
data.answer: Yes. A thin metal strip can bend and still be hard to dent. Hardness and flexibility are different properties. Shape and thickness matter too.

data.question: Where does plastic come from?
data.answer: Many plastics start with chemicals from oil or gas. Some use plants. Early plastics were made in the 1800s. More kinds came later.

data.question: Why do we still use wood? 🌳
data.answer: Wood can hold things up and be cut to shape. Its kind and thickness matter. Trees take time to grow. We can use wood again and care for forests.

data.question: Is glass really see-through all the way?
data.answer: Clear glass lets us see details. Frosted glass lets light through but blurs the view. Smooth does not always mean clear.

data.question: What is the strongest material? 💪
data.answer: Ask what the job needs. Pulling, pressing, scratching, and breaking are different tests. Shape and thickness matter too.

data.question: Can a material be used again?
data.answer: Reuse means use an object again. A jar can hold pencils. Recycling turns suitable old material into new products. Glass and metal may be melted. Paper is made into pulp. Check what your local program takes.

data.title: The Spill Test
data.instructions: Compare how three material samples behave with water. Predict first, keep the comparison fair, repeat, and describe your evidence. Do not decide a winner from wet-patch size.
data.fitReason: The standard asks students to plan an investigation and to use the data to pick a material for a purpose. A spill is a job second graders already understand, so the test is about the material and not about the setup.

brief.context: We have paper towel, cotton cloth, and a plastic sheet. A teacher cuts equal-size dry squares. We have trays, a spoon, water, and a timer.
brief.audience: The school office, who need to know which cloth to keep by the sink
brief.drivingQuestion: What happens when we put the same amount of water on each sample and wait the same time?
brief.seedDirection: Use equal-size dry samples and the same water amount. Wait the same time. Look on top and in the tray below. Repeat with fresh dry samples. A large wet patch does not prove more water went in.
lockedLessonFacts: Absorb means take liquid into a material.
A surface bead alone does not prove a material stays waterproof.
Keep sample size, water amount, waiting time, and method alike.
If two samples take in all the added water, this test does not show which could hold more.
openQuestions: What will we keep the same?
Do fresh samples act the same way?
stakeholders: The school office choosing a cloth
Your partner who pours the water
criteria: Use the same water amount and wait time
Predict first, then record what happened
constraints: Three sample materials in separate trays
Teacher-selected small equal water amounts and waiting time
No squeezing or rubbing; repeat with fresh dry samples
brief.deliverable: Draw what happened to each sample. Show water on top, in the cloth, or in the tray. Tell which job it might suit and what you still do not know.

parallelExample.context: A class compared dry paper, cloth, and plastic samples.
parallelExample.move: They kept sample size, water amount, and waiting time alike. They recorded surface water and damp areas, then repeated with fresh dry samples.
parallelExample.whyItHelps: Keeping conditions alike makes the comparison more useful. Their drawings record observations, not a guaranteed ranking of all papers, cloths, or plastics.

supports.frameStarter: I predicted ____. I observed ____. This evidence suggests ____, but it does not tell us ____.
coachPrompts: Did samples start dry and receive equal water amounts?
Did you wait the same time and check the tray below?
What cannot be concluded from a wet patch alone?

data.coachHint: Same size, dry start, same water and time. Repeat. Describe the evidence.
data.sourceExcerpt: Compare real samples under similar conditions. A wet patch shows spreading; its size alone does not measure the water absorbed.
